intro: Most writing advice online is quietly American, or quietly British, and never says so. That is a problem if you are applying for a job in Lagos, submitting to a journal in Melbourne, or writing to a client in Toronto. This section collects the conventions that actually differ by country — the ones that make a reader think "this wasn't written for us" without being able to say why.
principle: Match the destination, not your habit. Whatever variety you learned, the rule for any single piece of writing is the same: pick the convention of the place it is going, and apply it consistently from the first word to the last. A document that mixes -ise and -ize, or writes 03/04 without saying which month it means, costs the reader attention you needed for your argument.

topics.title: Spelling
topics.blurb: The differences are small, systematic and easy to apply once you know the four patterns.

rows.us: organize, realize, apologize
rows.note: Oxford University Press and most UK academic journals use -ize; UK newspapers, schools and general usage prefer -ise. Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, India, Nigeria and Kenya follow the -ise convention. Canada is split and leans -ize.

rows.us: color, honor, labor, favor
rows.note: The Commonwealth follows the UK almost universally. Canada keeps -our, unlike its other US-leaning habits.

rows.us: center, theater, meter, fiber
rows.note: Canada, Australia, Nigeria, India and Ireland follow the UK. In the US, "theatre" survives as a proper-noun spelling for arts venues.

rows.us: traveled, canceled, modeling
rows.note: UK doubles a final -l before a suffix regardless of stress; the US doubles it only when the last syllable is stressed. The Commonwealth follows the UK.

rows.us: license, practice, defense
rows.note: This one carries real meaning in UK usage: a driving licence is a thing, but an authority licenses a driver. Getting it wrong in a legal or professional document is noticed.

rows.us: gray, program, check (bank), tire, plow, aluminum
rows.uk: grey, programme (but computer program), cheque, tyre, plough, aluminium
rows.note: "Program" is the software exception in UK English and always has been. Aluminium has an extra i and an extra syllable outside North America.

topics.title: Dates and numbers
topics.blurb: The single most dangerous convention gap in international writing, because both readings look correct.

rows.us: 03/04/2026 means 4 March
rows.note: There is no way for a reader to tell which you meant. Write the month as a word — 3 April 2026 or April 3, 2026 — in anything that matters. For data and filenames use ISO 8601: 2026-04-03, which is unambiguous everywhere and sorts correctly.

rows.us: April 3, 2026 — comma required after the day
rows.note: Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa and India follow the UK order. Canada accepts both, which is its own kind of hazard.

The English-speaking world agrees here, but much of Europe, Latin America and Indonesia writes 1.234,56 — the separators are swapped. Never assume a number will be read as you wrote it in a translated or international document.

rows.us: 1,000,000 (one million)
rows.note: India and Pakistan also use lakh (100,000) and crore (10,000,000), with digit grouping as 10,00,000. Perfectly standard in Indian English; give the international figure alongside it when writing for a global audience.

rows.us: 6:00 p.m., 12-hour clock dominant
rows.uk: 18:00 or 6pm — 24-hour common in transport and official contexts
rows.note: The 24-hour clock is standard across most of continental Europe and in official use in much of Africa and Asia. If a meeting time can be misread by twelve hours, state the time zone too.

Always disambiguate the dollar: US$1,200, A$1,200, C$1,200, NZ$1,200 all read as "$". BRYME's opportunity listings state pay in the currency the publication states, because converting silently would misrepresent the offer.

topics.title: Letters and formal address
topics.blurb: Punctuation after a salutation, and how a letter closes, both differ — and both are visible at a glance.

rows.us: Dear Ms Okafor: — colon in business letters
rows.note: The US colon is genuinely formal usage, not an error. A comma is safe almost everywhere; a colon in a UK or Commonwealth letter looks slightly foreign.

rows.us: Mr., Mrs., Ms., Dr. — with full stops
rows.uk: Mr, Mrs, Ms, Dr — no full stops
rows.note: The UK omits the stop when the abbreviation ends with the word's last letter. The Commonwealth follows. Consistency matters more than the choice.

rows.us: Dear Hiring Manager, or Dear Sir or Madam
rows.uk: Dear Sir or Madam, closing with Yours faithfully
rows.note: In UK convention the close depends on the opening: a named recipient takes Yours sincerely, an unnamed one takes Yours faithfully. This pairing is still taught and still noticed. Find the name if you possibly can — it beats both.

rows.us: Sincerely, / Best regards, / Regards,
rows.uk: Yours sincerely, / Yours faithfully, / Kind regards,
rows.note: Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana, India and Pakistan generally follow the UK forms, often somewhat more formally than the UK now does.

rows.us: Warmer and quicker to first names, even in a first approach
rows.uk: More reserved on first contact; first names follow the recipient's lead
rows.note: Nigerian, Indian and Kenyan business correspondence tends to be more formal than either, and titles carry real weight. Erring formal costs you nothing; erring casual can cost you the reply.

rows.us: Recipient address top left, then date
rows.uk: Sender address top right, recipient left, then date
rows.note: Largely invisible in email, which is now most correspondence — but it still matters in a formal letter, a legal notice or a scanned attachment.

topics.title: Punctuation and quotation
topics.blurb: Quotation marks and the position of the full stop are the tells that reveal which side of the Atlantic you learned on.

rows.us: Double first: "she said"
rows.note: UK usage is genuinely mixed and house styles vary. Doubles are safe everywhere. Whatever you pick, nest the other kind inside.

rows.us: Inside: she said "maybe," and left.
rows.uk: Outside unless part of the quotation: she said 'maybe', and left.
rows.note: The UK rule is logical — only punctuate inside if the punctuation belonged to the original. The US rule is typographic and applies regardless. This is the single clearest marker of which variety a text follows.

rows.us: Standard in most US style guides: red, white, and blue
rows.uk: Usually omitted: red, white and blue
rows.note: Named after Oxford University Press, which uses it, in a country that mostly does not. Use it whenever its absence creates ambiguity — that exception is universal.

rows.us: e.g., i.e., etc. — with stops and often a following comma
rows.uk: eg, ie, etc — stops increasingly dropped
rows.note: Both are acceptable within their own conventions. Do not mix them in one document.

rows.us: Singular: the team is winning
rows.uk: Often plural: the team are winning
rows.note: The UK treats a collective as plural when the members act individually. Both are correct in their own variety; neither is an error.

topics.title: Job and study documents
topics.blurb: What is expected on a CV, and what is illegal to include, changes completely across borders.

rows.us: Résumé, one page, non-academic
rows.note: See the full comparison at /compare/cv-vs-resume/. Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana, India, South Africa, Australia and Ireland all say CV and mean the short document.

rows.us: Never — employers may discard the application
rows.note: Also avoid in Canada, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand. Conventional and often expected in Germany, much of continental Europe, and many employers in Nigeria, India and the Middle East.

rows.item: Date of birth, marital status, gender
rows.us: Never
rows.note: Same across the anglophone West for anti-discrimination reasons. Still routinely requested on application forms in parts of West Africa, South Asia and the Gulf. Supply what the form asks and nothing more.

rows.us: "References available on request" or omitted entirely
rows.uk: Two referees named, or available on request
rows.note: In Nigeria, Kenya and India it is common to name referees with full contact details on the CV itself. Ask permission first, wherever you are.

rows.us: GPA out of 4.0, included if strong
rows.note: Nigeria and India use First Class, Second Class Upper/Lower, or a CGPA out of 5.0, 7.0 or 10.0. Always state the scale — "3.8" means nothing without knowing the maximum.

rows.us: Application essay, prompt-driven, often several short ones
rows.uk: One UCAS statement, 4,000 characters, sent to every course
rows.note: A US application essay can be a personal narrative; a UCAS statement must be about the subject. They are not interchangeable.

topics.title: Pitching across cultures
topics.blurb: For writers approaching publications outside their own country — in both directions.

rows.us: Get to the idea in the first sentence. No throat-clearing.
rows.uk: Slightly more preamble tolerated, but not much.
rows.note: Writers trained in West African, South Asian or East Asian correspondence conventions are often taught to open with courtesy and build to the request. Western editors read the first sentence and decide. Lead with the idea; the courtesy can follow.

rows.us: State achievements plainly. Understatement reads as having none.
rows.uk: Plain statement, less superlative. Overselling reads as insecurity.
rows.note: The gap between "do not boast" as a cultural value and "state your qualifications" as a professional requirement is real. Facts are not boasting: "I have published in three national newspapers" is a fact.

rows.us: First names quickly. "Dear Sarah" after one exchange is normal.
rows.note: "Respected Sir/Madam" and "Kindly do the needful" are entirely standard in Indian and Nigerian professional English and are not errors — but to a US or UK editor they signal a template. Use the editor's name.

rows.us: Explain non-US context; do not assume knowledge.
rows.note: Your local knowledge is an asset, not a liability — it is often the reason you get commissioned. Explain the context in one clause rather than assuming it or apologising for it.

rows.us: Rates in US$, payment often 30 days after publication.
rows.note: Ask which rights you are selling and how payment reaches you. International transfer fees can consume a meaningful share of a small fee — settle the method before you file, not after.

rows.us: Submit in the publication's variety, consistently.
rows.note: No serious publication rejects work for being written in another variety of English, but a copy-editor will convert it and inconsistency creates work. Set your spellchecker to the destination before your final pass.
